title: Ἥλιος καὶ βάτραχοι
part: The Sun and the Frogs (Chambry 127 · Perry 314)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 127 (= Perry 314). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Γάμοι τοῦ Ἡλίου θέρους ἐγίγνοντο· πάντα δὲ τὰ ζῷα ἔχαιρον ἐπὶ τούτῳ, ἠγάλλοντο δὲ καὶ οἱ βάτραχοι.
sentences.tr: Gamoi tou Hēliou therous egignonto· panta de ta zōia echairon epi toutōi, ēgallonto de kai hoi batrachoi.
sentences.l: The wedding of the Sun was taking place in summer; and all the animals rejoiced at this, and the frogs too exulted.
sentences.n: γάμοι is regularly plural for a single wedding — the many days and rites of it. θέρους is the genitive of the time within which, 'in the course of the summer'. ἐπί with the dative gives what one rejoices at.

sentences.t: Εἷς δὲ τούτων εἶπεν· « Ὦ μῶροι, εἰς τί ἀγάλλεσθε ; εἰ γὰρ μόνος ὢν ὁ Ἥλιος πᾶσαν ἰλὺν ἀποξηραίνει, εἰ γήμας ὅμοιον αὐτῷ παιδίον γεννήσει, τί οὐ πάθωμεν κακόν ; »
sentences.tr: Heis de toutōn eipen· « Ō mōroi, eis ti agallesthe ; ei gar monos ōn ho Hēlios pasan ilyn apoxērainei, ei gēmas homoion autōi paidion gennēsei, ti ou pathōmen kakon ; »
sentences.l: But one of them said: « O fools, to what end do you exult? For if the Sun, being but one, dries up every mire, if, having married, he shall beget a child like himself, what evil shall we not suffer? »
sentences.n: ἰλύς is the wet mud at the bottom of a pool — the frogs' own element, which is why the Sun's heat is their affair and no one else's. Two conditions in a row: the first with the plain present indicative, stating what already happens; the second with the future indicative, the shape Greek uses for a threat or a warning. πάθωμεν is a deliberative subjunctive, 'what are we to suffer?', and the οὐ shapes the question so that it expects no answer but 'every evil there is'. Chambry's house punctuation puts a space before the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: Ὅτι πολλοὶ τῶν τὸ φρόνημα κουφότερον ἐχόντων χαίρουσιν ἐπὶ πράγμασιν τοῖς μὴ χαρὰν ἔχουσιν.
sentences.tr: Hoti polloi tōn to phronēma kouphoteron echontōn chairousin epi pragmasin tois mē charan echousin.
sentences.l: That many of those who have a rather light mind rejoice at things that have no joy in them.
sentences.i: The story shows that many of those who have a rather light mind rejoice at things that have no joy in them.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. φρόνημα is the settled cast of a person's thought; κουφότερον is a comparative with nothing to compare to, so 'rather light, on the light side'. The μή before the participle marks a class of thing rather than a particular one — 'things of the kind that hold no joy'.
